newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Aluminium producers say no to new MOU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Aluminium producers say no to new MOU.

text.p: Speculation that a new Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) among leading aluminium producing nations was on the cards was quashed on Monday by most of the signatories to the original output-cutting deal.

Government spokesmen in Australia, Canada and Norway all said they were unaware of any plans to renew the 1994 MOU which expired earlier this year. What is more likely instead is co-operation on providing statistics.
"There will not be another MOU, simply a working group," Canada's International Trade Department spokesman Sanjeev Chowdhury said on Friday.

In Moscow on Monday the Kontsern Alyuminiy producers' association said Russia's aluminium producers have agreed not to increase output from current levels, but will not make cuts in existing production levels.
Other countries had agreed to do the same.

"There is no agreement to cut output, but there is an agreement, taken at board level at the smelters, not to bring on line new capacity that is not now being used," said Igor Prokopov, adding that 80,000-100,000 tonnes of currently unused capacity would not be activated.
However, Australia's Aluminium Development Council executive director David Coutts said the council was not pushing to restrain production and knew of no moves by Russia.
Meanwhile, Norway said it was not in talks with other goverments.
Lars Olaf Selnes, advisor in the industrial policy department in the Ministry of Industry and Energy, said there had been no contacts on a governmental level since the MOU ran out earlier this year.
Industry officials and analysts here were dubious, as there has been no inkling that a new production cutting accord was being discussed.
"The fact is that Russia is already producing at relatively high levels and it is highly questionable whether the money is available to cut production anyway," brokers GNI Ltd said.

Cuts by the Russian smelters are also unlikely, even though production costs are high, due to the need for foreign exchange earnings and the necessity of providing employment for workers in remote locations, analysts said.

Signatories to the two-year MOU, which was signed in March 1994, were the European Union, Norway, Australia, the United States, Canada and Russia. The deal aimed to cut output by 10 percent and reduce bloated inventories.
Much of the capacity in the United States, Canada, and France idled under this accord remains shut, with a U.S. Justice department anti-trust probe into the MOU still on-going.

The London Metal Exchange (LME) aluminium market was unimpressed by the speculation of the last few days, with three months prices hardly moving from around $1,330. Last week, the LME was at 2-1/2 year lows of $1,305/tonne.
